tip: Liking lands on you in Hindi – मुझे पसंद है (mujhe pasand hai) is literally 'to me it is pleasing'. The liker takes मुझे, never मैं.
आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई (aapse milkar khushi hui) is literally 'having met you, happiness happened' – joy is an event that occurs, not something you are.
Prices use 'of': यह कितने का है? (yah kitne ka hai) = 'this is of how much?'. The answer keeps का too – सौ का है (sau ka hai) = it's a hundred.
ठीक-ठाक (theek-thaak) doubles ठीक with a rhyming echo to soften it – 'more or less fine'. Hindi loves these pairs: चाय-वाय (chai-vai) = tea and such.
Respect makes one person plural: पिताजी ... हैं (pitaji ... hain), not है – father gets the 'they' verb even though he is one man.
You don't miss someone – their memory comes to you: तुम्हारी याद आ रही थी (tumhari yaad aa rahi thi) = 'your memory was coming'.
Weddings happen rather than being gotten: शादी हुई थी (shaadi hui thi) = 'the wedding happened'. Hindi treats marrying as an event, with होना (hona = happen).
मिली (mili) is 'met' doing duty for 'found': the shop met you – दुकान मिली (dukaan mili). Things you find, get, or receive all 'meet' you in Hindi.
Hindi says how things got there: किताबें रखी हैं (kitaaben rakhi hain) = 'the books are kept'. Where English uses plain 'are', Hindi adds the placing verb.
Question words don't jump to the front: कितनी दूर (kitni door = how far) sits right where the answer would – स्टेशन कितनी दूर है, no flipping around.
Hindi's 'across' follows its noun: नदी के उस पार (nadi ke us paar) = 'the river's far side'. Position words come after the noun, not before it.
Age is something you are 'of': पचहत्तर साल के हैं (pachhattar saal ke hain) = 'is of seventy-five years'. No word for 'old' anywhere – के carries it.
No 'a' or 'an' in Hindi: इंजीनियर बनना (engineer banna) = 'to become engineer'. Articles don't exist – context does that work.
बैठी है (baithi hai) = 'is seated', a settled state. बैठ रही है would mean she is in the middle of sitting down. English '-ing' misleads here.
'By car' is 'having sat in the car': गाड़ी में बैठकर (gaadi mein baithkar). The -कर (-kar) ending chains actions – sit, then go, in one sentence.
भी (bhi = even, also) follows the word it highlights: तूफ़ान में भी (toofan mein bhi) = 'even in the storm'. English puts 'even' first; Hindi tags it after.
का matches the thing owned, not the owner: भाई का कमरा (bhai ka kamra) – का is masculine because कमरा is. Own a गाड़ी instead and it flips to की.
'Bring' is built from 'take' plus 'come': बाज़ार से ले आना (bazaar se le aana) = take from the market and come. ले जाना (le jaana = take plus go) is 'take away' – the second verb sets the direction.
Pills are eaten in Hindi: गोली खाने से (goli khaane se) = 'from eating the pill'. खाना stretches past food – even betrayal gets eaten: धोखा खाना (dhokha khaana) = to be betrayed.
गिर गई (gir gayi) adds जाना (jaana = go) to the fall – it marks the action as complete and final. Tacking जाना onto a verb means fully done.
'Have to' is built with 'to me': मुझे ... मिलना है (mujhe milna hai) = 'to me is to-meet'. Obligation sits on you as मुझे + verb + है.
कराई (karai) is causative – having it done, not doing it: रिपोर्ट दर्ज कराई = got the report registered, via the police. करना (karna) = do, कराना (karana) = have done.
साढ़े (saadhe) = 'plus a half': साढ़े तीन सौ (saadhe teen sau) = three and a half hundreds = 350 – not 'three hundred fifty'.
Useful things 'come to work': छाता बहुत काम आता है (kaam aata hai) = 'the umbrella comes to use'. काम आना is the everyday way to say something helps.
Rain is a thing that happens, not a verb: बारिश हो रही है (baarish ho rahi hai) = 'rain is happening'. There is no verb 'to rain' – बारिश is a noun and होना (hona) does the work.
के पास (ke paas) here is 'near': घर के पास = near the house. With a person it means having – मेरे पास किताब है (mere paas kitaab hai) = I have a book.
The plain -ना form makes a gentle, do-it-later request: भेज देना (bhej dena) = 'send it (when you get to it)'. Softer and less immediate than भेजो (bhejo).
Visibility is given in Hindi: दिखाई देता है (dikhai deta hai) = 'gives being-seen'. The city is the giver and you receive the view.
रख दो (rakh do) adds देना (dena = give) to the putting – the दो marks it as fully done, often for someone else's benefit. Plain रखो (rakho) is just 'put'.
Every number up to 100 is its own word: छत्तीस (chhattis = 36) is not built from 'thirty' plus 'six'. All hundred get memorized one by one.
पाँच बजे (paanch baje) = 'five having rung' – clock time counts bell strikes. बजना (bajna) means to ring, so 'at five' is literally five chimes.
You do someone's waiting: मेरा इंतज़ार करना (mera intezaar karna) = 'do my waiting'. The person waited for becomes a possessive, not 'for me'.
भीगते हुए (bheegte hue) = 'while getting soaked' – the -ते हुए ending runs one action in the background while the main one happens.
The minutes do the taking: दस मिनट लगते हैं (das minute lagte hain) = 'ten minutes attach'. With लगना (lagna), time is the subject – nobody takes it.
होने वाली है (hone wali hai) = 'is about to happen'. वाला after a verb means on-the-verge – closer and more certain than plain future tense.
There's no 'there is' – just है at the end: सड़क पर बहुत ट्रैफ़िक है (sadak par bahut traffic hai) = 'on the road much traffic is'.
बिना (bina = without) wraps its phrase from both ends: बिना किसी की मदद के (bina kisi ki madad ke) – बिना opens, के closes. Don't drop the closing के.
जी (ji) after a name adds warm respect: गौरव जी (Gaurav ji). It even works alone – a plain जी is a polite 'yes?'.
You talk 'from' a person: डॉक्टर से (doctor se) = with the doctor. से stretches across English 'with', 'from', and 'by' – the verb decides which.
Hindi has no word for cousin – cousins are siblings with a tag: मौसेरे भाई-बहन (mausere bhai-behen) = brothers and sisters via your mother's sister.
Grandfathers split by side: दादाजी (dadaji) is your father's father, नानाजी (nanaji) your mother's father. One English word, two Hindi people.
